Therapy Culture Has Gone Too Far, Says a Stanford Psychiatrist66 min37 insights2026-11-03
▶ Watch on YouTube
Stanford psychiatrist Anna Lembke (Dopamine Nation, Radical Surrender) tells Scott Galloway that technology-enabled micro-control has made people more anxious, that digital media are drugs fueling an 'addiction economy' (alcohol falling as sports betting, porn, gaming and shopping addictions rise), and that therapy culture has become too inward and backward. She prescribes one-hour social media caps, embodied/trade education, behavioral contracts for non-launching young men, and outward-facing virtue.

Paradox of control and anxiety 6
Stanford psychiatrist Anna Lembke argues that the more levers for micro-control technology gives people over their lives, the more anxious, fearful, lonely and bored they become.
thesis🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: highStanford
So what: Products sold on promises of control and optimization may be deepening the anxiety they claim to relieve.
“the more levers for microcontrol that we have over our lives uh the more anxious, fearful uh and uh lonely I would argue as well as bored we've become” ▶ 2:27
Lembke says abundant choice makes young people fear that a single wrong choice means missing their 'best life', and when things go wrong they blame only themselves, producing shame and self-loathing.
causal🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: high
So what: Choice overload is a mental-health driver, not just a consumer-UX issue.
Lembke reports more young people self-harming or ending their lives after relatively minor failures such as social rejection or an academic reprimand that a generation ago would have been tolerable.
data_point🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: medium
So what: Signals a falling threshold for distress tolerance among youth.
Lembke describes over-protective parenting as codependent: parents insulate kids from pain and uncertainty largely to reduce their own anxiety, producing a generation with no tolerance for uncertainty and no psychological template for resilience.
causal🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: high
So what: Parenting style is a root cause upstream of screens.
Lembke argues that tracking devices (e.g., baby breathing monitors, child trackers) feed obsessive reassurance-seeking loops, and as with OCD, more reassurance makes people more anxious.
causal🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: mediumOCD
So what: Monitoring/surveillance products for parents may worsen the anxiety they monetize.
“the more we look for and get reassurance, the more OCD or anxious we become” ▶ 7:32
Lembke observes that even highly gifted Stanford students are sent reeling by small uncertainties or hints of imperfection.
anecdote🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: mediumStanford
So what: Elite achievement does not inoculate against low distress tolerance.
Digital media as drug: the addiction economy 11
Lembke states social media platforms are potent drugs, more potent than TV because users can micro-control consumption (swipe, scroll, tap) which hits the brain's dopamine reward pathway in the nucleus accumbens, the same one drugs and alcohol activate.
thesis🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: highsocial mediadopaminenucleus accumbens
So what: The 'TV was also the idiot box' analogy understates the risk.
“These platforms are not just powerful tools. They're also very potent drugs.” ▶ 9:51
Lembke reframes addiction as fundamentally about asserting control over moment-to-moment experience to change how one feels, not escaping control.
framework🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: medium
So what: Explains why the most controllable media are the most addictive.
“Addiction is all about control” ▶ 10:21
Lembke says children removed from devices show classic withdrawal (anxiety, irritability, insomnia, depression, craving, plus headaches, stomach aches, tantrums), but it is time-limited and kids typically re-emerge within a couple of days in a safe container.
data_point🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: high
So what: Digital detox interventions can show fast, visible results for families.
Lembke cites a growing body of evidence that capping emotionally distressed youths' objectively-measured social media use at one hour a day reduces depression and anxiety and improves sleep, loneliness and FOMO versus controls.
data_point🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: highsocial media
So what: A one-hour cap is an evidence-backed, actionable dose threshold.

Endemic narcissism and remedies 4
Lembke says the deepest human desire is connection; likes, followers and now AI chatbots that flatter users deliver social validation that releases dopamine, so people may no longer even need other humans for affirmation.
causal🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: mediumAI

“AI agents are completely engineered to do that for us” ▶ 54:18
Lembke describes an age of 'endemic narcissism' in which shame and self-loathing act as a natural homeostatic ballast for self-focused achievement, explaining widespread impostor syndrome.
framework🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: medium
So what: Status-seeking and self-loathing are linked rather than opposites.
Lembke's practical prescription against validation addiction: turn off likes, don't read comments (outsource if necessary), turn off self-view, and don't over-invest in appearance.
framework🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: medium

framework🗣 Dr. Anna Lembkeconviction: mediumRadical Surrender

A post-midterm VC roundtable (Jason Calacanis, DA Wallik, Elana Gold, Tomas of Theory Ventures) argues a Democratic House+Senate sweep makes data centers and AV politically toxic but reduces Trump-driven macro uncertainty, while a narrowing M&A window, GPU scarcity (Blackwell rental up ~120% to ~$13/hr) and possible AI rationing in 2027 reshape tech. Invest Like the Best · Patrick O'Shaughnessy 1 episode(s) · 42 insights

What Happens When the AI Boom Slows Down75 min42 insights2026-11-04
▶ Watch on YouTube
Infrastructure VC Martin Casado (who sold his networking company to VMware) argues investors conflate four incompatible mindsets (financial, productive, frontier, speculative), that defensibility debates matter little in growing markets, and that AI's real disruption is that capital can now be converted directly into engineering output. The title's question is addressed directly: if the AI market saturates, frontier labs' pricing power and 3-6 month model lifespans could send value 'crashing back down into open source'; he also covers debt scarcity for NeoClouds, hardware/power as the true constraint, data-center regulation, and lessons from the Cursor, World Labs and Open Router strategic M&A deals.
Four investor mindsets & disruptive-tech diligence · 6Moats: shape vs mechanism, and why defensibility is overrated · 5Frontier models if the AI market slows · 7Infrastructure stack refactored by AI · 6Capital as the new input: debt, compute, NeoClouds, data centers · 7Private-market efficiency and capital creating TAM · 4Strategic M&A playbook (Cursor, World Labs, Open Router) · 5AI as general technology, not software · 2
Four investor mindsets & disruptive-tech diligence 6
Casado sorts private-tech investors into four mindsets: financial (market size and SaaS metrics as proxy for the business), productive (the technical asset creates value and the market follows), frontier (back founders' visions with little diligence, 'yolo'), and speculative (timing prices without caring about the asset).
framework🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: highventure capital
So what: Identify which mindset a co-investor or board member holds before debating a deal; each justifies different conclusions.
“I think there's basically four types of mindsets” ▶ 1:00
Because each of the four mindsets is internally coherent, an investor who does not know their own framework can justify or reject any deal and ends up rationalizing personal bias.
causal🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: high
So what: Process discipline: write down the investing framework before diligence to avoid post-hoc justification.
“if you don't know what your beliefs are, you'll always basically just kind of justify whatever personal bias you have” ▶ 3:23
Applying a financial mindset (quality of revenue, TAM, NRR) to early disruptive technology is incoherent, because disruptive tech creates its own TAM and business models always lag disruptive technologies.
contrarian🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: highinternetcloudmobile
So what: Early-stage investors screening on revenue quality will systematically drift toward non-disruptive companies.
“business models always lag disruptive technologies” ▶ 17:35
Every tech wave (internet, mobile, cloud, and now AI) has seen hand-wringing about margins before the COGS and business model were figured out; early willingness-to-pay is a partial indicator that can justify investment before unit economics exist.
framework🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: highAIcloudmobileinternet
So what: Current worries about AI gross margins are historically normal and not by themselves a reason to avoid the category.
As a productive infrastructure investor, Casado's diligence does not second-guess founders' tech but asks how it fits into broader platforms, spending budgets, stickiness, and what leading companies are building internally; he accepts early numbers 'a financial investor would puke at'.
framework🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: high
So what: Look for adjacent growing budgets and what large platforms build in-house as leading indicators of new infra categories.
Venture has partly morphed into public-style investing because private companies now rival public companies of 10-20 years ago (Stripe, Databricks, Anduril, SpaceX pre-IPO), and many entrants came from business-school/finance backgrounds, so later-stage instincts get applied too early.
causal🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: mediumStripeDatabricksAndurilSpaceX
So what: Expect friction on early-stage boards where growth/PE investors over-rotate on burn and metrics.
Moats: shape vs mechanism, and why defensibility is overrated 5
'Network effect' appears on roughly 70% of pitch decks yet has no consensus definition; the common definition (product gets better with each marginal user) is nearly tautological and says nothing about defensibility.
data_point🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: mediumnetwork effects
So what: Press founders claiming network effects to specify the mechanism and how it scales.
“you have this very common word that's on 70% of pitch decks where a founder is sitting in front doing a pitch and nobody has consensus on what it means” ▶ 7:28
Moat analysis should separate the mechanism (brand, scale, two-sided marketplace, network effect) from the shape of the moat with scale (superlinear, linear, sublinear); only superlinear moats let a leader outgrow an equally funded challenger, while sublinear moats mean challengers always catch up.
framework🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: highMetcalfe's law
So what: Assess whether a leader's marginal dollar buys more growth than a challenger's; if not, leadership is not durable.
“we conflate the mechanism with the shape of the moat” ▶ 7:47
True superlinear (Metcalfe-style) network effects are rare, with examples like the telcos, LinkedIn and GitHub (interconnections of users); Uber is better described as a funding-driven scale effect because drivers and riders multi-home.
contrarian🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: mediumLinkedInGitHubUber
So what: Discount 'network effect' valuations for marketplaces where both sides multi-home.
“all drivers drive for everybody and all passengers could use anybody” ▶ 14:18
Defensibility is a second- or third-order concern in growing markets because competitors move into new white space rather than fight, and shrinking markets consolidate regardless of moats; investors who refused to back foundation models or NeoClouds as 'not defensible' were wrong because the market grew.
contrarian🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: highNeoCloudsfoundation models
So what: In AI infra, prioritize market growth rate over moat analysis when deciding whether to invest.
“I think that we kind of trick ourselves as investors by thinking in terms of defensibility when if there's a growing market, it's kind of not even worth considering” ▶ 15:43
Moat analysis cannot be done in isolation because it is about competitive equilibria: a better-capitalized competitor with its own network effect can change the shape of your moat.
framework🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: medium
So what: Factor competitors' funding capacity into any durability assessment.
Frontier models if the AI market slows 7
For three years, frontier models that are even marginally better have captured 80%+ of dollar-weighted market share with tremendous pricing power and effectively infinite demand, because the market is far from saturated.
data_point🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: highfrontier modelsAnthropic
So what: Frontier-lab economics are fine as long as AI spend keeps growing; the key risk variable is saturation.
“these kind of frontier models that are the best tend to get 80% plus of the market dollar weighted and that's happened for 3 years” ▶ 25:25
Enterprise AI penetration is roughly 3% by adoption but about 1% or less by budget, leaving a long growth runway.
data_point🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: mediumenterprise AI
So what: Supports a long-duration AI spend cycle before saturation dynamics bite.
“They say 3% of the enterprise, but actually from budget- wise, it's like 1% or less” ▶ 25:53
From app-company data and pitches, the commercial lifespan of a frontier model is only 3-6 months, so a lab that slips a release (e.g., Anthropic stumbling for six months due to regulatory, technical or breach issues) could lose most of its market, unlike software's long tail of retention.
data_point🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: highAnthropic
So what: Model labs carry release-cadence risk that standard software valuation models (long-tail retention) fail to capture.
“I would say that the lifespan of a model is three to six months” ▶ 27:03
If AI use cases saturate or market growth slows, there is a very real scenario where value 'comes crashing back down into open source' and frontier labs lose pricing power.
prediction🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: exploratoryopen sourcefrontier models
So what: Key bear case for frontier-lab valuations (e.g., Anthropic S-1 buyers) is saturation, not competition per se.
“I think there's a very real world where this the value comes crashing back down into open source” ▶ 27:31
Even if coding tasks are ~95% automated so token volume stops growing, firms will not switch to cheaper models, because in competitive equilibria a company always pays 10x more for the smartest model to beat rivals; pricing is maintained even if volume slows.
contrarian🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: highfrontier modelscoding
So what: Saturation of tasks does not imply commoditization of frontier pricing while firms compete on software quality and speed.
“You would always pay 10 times more for the smartest model” ▶ 28:53
Anthropic and OpenAI have probably raised more money in aggregate than their entire downstream ecosystem combined, functioning as mechanisms for turning money into growth.
data_point🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: mediumAnthropicOpenAI
So what: Capital concentration at the model layer makes lab funding conditions a systemic variable for AI.
Anything that can be simulated on a computer can have RL environments built for it, so Casado considers the digital side 'done' (AI will be able to do anything done on a computer), while it is unknown whether the same scaling curves apply to robotics, science and medicine.
thesis🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: highreinforcement learningrobotics

“I feel very comfortable that the current the current the digital side is done” ▶ 35:47

Capital as the new input: debt, compute, NeoClouds, data centers 7
AI's industrial-revolution-level shift is that capital can be thrown at problems: unlike the Mythical Man-Month era where adding engineers slowed projects, 20 people can now productively use a billion dollars.
thesis🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: highMythical Man-MonthFred Brooks
So what: Capital allocators become direct drivers of innovation; expect ever-larger rounds into small AI teams.
“I can take 20 people and I can give them a billion dollars and they can use that” ▶ 43:36
Debt is running out for non-investment-grade AI infrastructure: a fund like Norway's pension would rather buy T-bills than lend to a random NeoCloud, so scale players win and smaller players will need customers to prepay.
prediction🗣 Martin Casadoconviction: mediumNeoCloudsNorway pension fundT-bills
So what: Debt-dependent NeoCloud business models face financing stress; customer prepayments become a key metric.

Aztec co-founder Zac Williamson tells Bankless's David Hoffman that Aztec is the only privacy-preserving smart contract chain besides Zcash (which offers private money rather than smart contracts) with no protocol-level backdoors or viewing keys. He argues that privacy will win as a requirement rather than a feature. On his account it enables compliant, composable on-chain RWAs and identity (ZK Passport) instead of today's siloed 'off-chain mega apps', and AI-driven exploits will push activity onto formally verified, trustless infrastructure. He outlines the Aztec Tiara upgrade (proving time halved, 6-12s soft finality) and 2027 goals (5-minute hard finality, real-time proving).

How Private Jets Are About to Become More Affordable29 min20 insights2026-11-03

Joe Lonsdale interviews Tal Keinan, CEO of Sky Harbor (SKYH), on the structural shortage of private-aircraft hangars at US general aviation airports: no new airports, federal subsidies exclude hangars, and the Signature/Atlantic FBO duopoly prioritizes fuel-heavy charter traffic. Keinan explains Sky Harbor's 'home base operator' model financed by tax-exempt private activity bonds at ~4.2-4.75% fixed, AI-driven tenant targeting, and the thesis that AI-created wealth (and big IPOs) will expand private-aviation demand; the title's affordability claim is Lonsdale's long-run view rather than a near-term mechanism discussed.

The US has the densest airport infrastructure in the world, largely built in the 1930s-40s as a New Deal employment scheme, but no new airports will be built because where there is need there is no land and vice versa.
